fixes.explanation: That's the one. God tells Moses, Israel's leader, “…as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them.” (Exodus 6:3) So Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Israel's forefathers, knew Him as God Almighty. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you hearing your own name again is a gift.

God Most High sounds mighty and holy, and I see why it tempts you. But in Exodus 6:3 God says He appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty. That's the name He gives there. He also says He did not make Himself known to them by His name the LORD.

The Everlasting God is a lovely name, friend. But it isn't the one in this verse. God tells Moses He appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, and that He did not make Himself known to them by His name the LORD (Exodus 6:3).

Yes, foreigners. God calls Canaan “…the land where they lived as foreigners.” (Exodus 6:4) Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Israel's forefathers, lived in the very land God promised to give them. I think that makes the promise feel even bigger.
Rulers isn't what the verse says, baker. God calls Canaan “…the land where they lived as foreigners.” (Exodus 6:4) His covenant was to give them that land. So the word the verse uses is foreigners.

Right, groaning. God says, “Furthermore, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving…” (Exodus 6:5) He says He heard it, and He says He has remembered His covenant. Friend, I know what it's like to be stuck in the dark, and I'm glad that's what the verse says.

A feast sounds nice, friend, but this verse has no table in it. The Egyptians are enslaving the Israelites, and God says He has heard their groaning (Exodus 6:5). That's the sound He names. Feasting isn't in the verse.

Yes! God says, “I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God.” (Exodus 6:7) The leaving is only part of it. He is also taking them as His own. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so being wanted means a lot to me.

Yes, speech. Moses says he is “…unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) I think he's nervous about talking to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Friend, I'd be nervous too, because my best speech so far is mumbling through a mustache.
Moses doesn't bring up fighting here. He says he is “…unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) I think his concern is about talking to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Battle isn't part of what he says.
Writing isn't what Moses says, baker. He says he is “…unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) I think his concern is about standing up and talking to Pharaoh. That's talking, not writing.

That's backwards, baker. God tells Moses to tell Pharaoh “…everything I say to you.” (Exodus 6:29) Later He says Moses is to speak all He commands, and Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:2). Nothing in either verse hands the wording over to Aaron.

Yes, prophet. God tells Moses, “…your brother Aaron will be your prophet.” (Exodus 7:1) Aaron, Moses' brother, is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land (Exodus 7:2). Moses had said he was unskilled in speech, and I think a brother at his side must have been welcome news.

A bodyguard is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the job. God says, “…your brother Aaron will be your prophet.” (Exodus 7:1) Aaron's part is speaking, since he is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:2). Guarding isn't in the verse.

Search is a heart word, baker, but it isn't the one here. In Exodus 7:3 God says, “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart…” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and that's what God says about him. So the answer is harden.

Not quite, baker. God says that though He will multiply His signs and wonders, “Pharaoh will not listen to you.” (Exodus 7:3-4) So the answer is false. Then He says He will lay His hand on Egypt and bring His people out by mighty acts of judgment.

False is right. Even with His signs and wonders multiplying, God says, “Pharaoh will not listen to you.” (Exodus 7:3-4) Then He says, “…by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 7:4) So Pharaoh not listening is part of what God tells Moses, and He still says what He will do.

True. “So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.” (Exodus 7:6) Moses had said twice that he was unskilled in speech (Exodus 6:12, 6:30). I bet that wasn't easy, but they did just as He said. Friend, that's an ending I'd frame.

It's true, baker. The text says, “So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.” (Exodus 7:6) Moses had said he was unskilled in speech, and I bet he felt nervous. They still did it. I know a thing or two about doing something when you're nervous.

Eighty. “Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.” (Exodus 7:7) That's Moses' age at the moment the two of them speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Aaron, his brother, is eighty-three. That's a lot of years behind two men walking in to speak to a king.

Yes, eighty-three. The text says, “Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.” (Exodus 7:7) So Aaron, Moses' brother, is three years older than Moses. Three years apart, and the two of them walk in to speak to Pharaoh together.
